meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The price of freedom is eternal vigilance'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Jefferson. Monticello lists it as spurious; the idea traces to J.P. Curran (1790) and Wendell Phillips (1852). 'Freedom' is a modern variant of 'liberty.'

answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — a misattribution
answer.authorName: John Philpot Curran (idea) & Wendell Phillips (popular form)
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Jefferson ever wrote or spoke this line; Monticello lists it among his spurious quotations ↗. The thought traces to Irish orator John Philpot Curran, who in a Dublin speech of 10 July 1790 said “the condition upon which God hath given liberty to man is eternal vigilance,” and the compact aphorism — in its “liberty” form — was made famous by abolitionist Wendell Phillips in 1852. The wording “price of freedom” is a still-later paraphrase.

trail: Not Jefferson. Monticello’s Jefferson quotations archive files it as a spurious quotation ↗, saying it does not appear in his writings.
Traces to Curran, 1790. Per This Day in Quotes ↗, the earliest kindred line is John Philpot Curran’s Dublin speech of 10 July 1790.

Popularized by Wendell Phillips, 1852. The same research notes Phillips’ address to the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society (28 Jan 1852) as the most-cited source of the modern aphorism, with the “price of liberty” form already in print by 1809.
‘Freedom’ is a variant. The standard wording is “price of liberty”; the “price of freedom” phrasing is a later, unsourced paraphrase.
source.excerptNote: Wendell Phillips’ 1852 line is the most-cited source of the modern aphorism. The submitted wording — “The price of freedom is eternal vigilance” — swaps “freedom” for “liberty” and reverses the clauses; no primary source ties that exact form to Jefferson or anyone else.

author.name: John Philpot Curran
author.heading: Whose idea it really was
author.bio: John Philpot Curran was one of Ireland’s great courtroom orators and a defender of the United Irishmen. In a Dublin speech on 10 July 1790 he declared that “the condition upon which God hath given liberty to man is eternal vigilance” — the sentiment from which the modern aphorism descends. The neat English maxim “eternal vigilance is the price of liberty” was later put into wide circulation by American abolitionist Wendell Phillips in 1852; neither man was Thomas Jefferson.

cite.sourceCitation: John Philpot Curran, speech at the election of the Lord Mayor of Dublin, 10 July 1790 (“the condition upon which God hath given liberty to man is eternal vigilance”); modern aphorism popularized in Wendell Phillips, address to the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society, 28 January 1852. Listed as spurious to Jefferson by the Thomas Jefferson Foundation (Monticello).

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s most reliable false-Jefferson quotes. Its true lineage is Irish and abolitionist, not Monticellan.

items.why: Monticello’s Jefferson archive lists it among spurious quotations ↗; it appears nowhere in his writings, and scholars find no evidence he ever used it.
Per documented provenance ↗, Curran’s 1790 Dublin speech — “the condition upon which God hath given liberty to man is eternal vigilance” — is the earliest kindred phrasing.

His 28 January 1852 address to the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society — “Eternal vigilance is the price of liberty; power is ever stealing from the many to the few” — is the most-cited source of the modern maxim, per This Day in Quotes ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: not Jefferson — the idea is John Philpot Curran’s (1790) and the famous wording is Wendell Phillips’ (1852), with “freedom” a modern swap for “liberty,” as Monticello confirms ↗.

context.heading: Why the mix-up
lead: Jefferson is a magnet for stirring civic one-liners, and the phrase’s themes — liberty, watchfulness, the danger of concentrated power — sound Jeffersonian. But the paper trail runs elsewhere. American newspapers first printed Curran’s 1790 words with his name, then began dropping the attribution and compressing the sentence, so that by the mid-19th century it circulated as a free-floating maxim ripe for reassignment to a Founding Father.

The wording submitted here, “the price of freedom is eternal vigilance,” is a second-order paraphrase: it reverses the clauses of the standard saying and swaps “freedom” for “liberty.” No primary source ties that exact phrasing to Jefferson — or to any single author.
context.pull: The idea is Curran’s, the famous wording is Phillips’, and neither man was Jefferson.
